title: Finance U3·W3 — Working Capital & the Cash Conversion Cycle
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the cash caught in operations

A profitable firm can still run out of cash. The reason is working capital — the cash tied up in inventory and receivables before customers pay, net of what suppliers finance. Managing it well frees cash and lowers the financing a growing business needs (the AFN from last week). This chapter covers net working capital, the cash conversion cycle, and the management of cash, receivables, inventory, and payables — the day-to-day finance that separates a solvent contractor from one that bounces payroll despite a full backlog.

Working capital defined

Working capital is the firm's short-term resources and obligations. Net working capital (NWC) = current assets − current liabilities; it measures the liquidity cushion funding day-to-day operations. Working-capital policy balances two risks: too little (illiquidity — the inability to pay obligations as they come due) and too much (idle assets earning no return). The art is holding just enough inventory, receivables, and cash to operate smoothly while financing them as cheaply as the risk allows.

The operating cycle and cash conversion cycle

Two cycles describe how cash moves through operations. The operating cycle is the time from acquiring inventory to collecting cash from its sale: days inventory outstanding (DIO) + days sales outstanding (DSO). The cash conversion cycle (CCC) subtracts the financing suppliers provide: CCC = DIO + DSO − days payable outstanding (DPO). The CCC is the number of days the firm's own cash is tied up. Worked example: DIO 60 days + DSO 45 days − DPO 30 days = 75 days of cash locked in the cycle. Shortening any component frees cash.

Computing the components

Each component is a turnover-based ratio. DIO = inventory ÷ (COGS ÷ 365) — how long inventory sits. DSO = accounts receivable ÷ (sales ÷ 365) — how long customers take to pay. DPO = accounts payable ÷ (COGS ÷ 365) — how long the firm takes to pay suppliers. A firm reduces its CCC by turning inventory faster, collecting receivables sooner, or (carefully) paying suppliers later. For a contractor, retainage and slow owner payments stretch DSO dramatically, which is why construction is so working-capital-intensive — the CCC concept directly explains the cash strain.

Cash management

Firms hold cash for the transaction, precautionary, and (less so) speculative motives, but idle cash earns little, so the goal is a target balance that meets needs without excess. Managers accelerate collections (lockboxes, electronic payment) and manage disbursement timing, exploiting — within ethical limits — the float between when a payment is recorded and when cash actually moves. A cash budget (the 13-week forecast a CFO lives by) projects inflows and outflows to reveal shortfalls before they happen — the link between working-capital management and the cash forecasting in the CFO lane.

Receivables and inventory

Receivables management sets the credit policy — to whom credit is granted, the terms (e.g., 2/10 net 30), and the collection effort — trading higher sales against the cost of carrying and potentially losing receivables. A cash discount like 2/10 net 30 carries a steep implicit annual cost if not taken, so customers usually should pay early and firms should evaluate offering it. Inventory management balances ordering costs against carrying costs — the economic order quantity (EOQ) minimizes their total — while just-in-time systems cut inventory (and DIO) by coordinating closely with suppliers. Both aim to support sales with the least cash tied up.

Payables and short-term financing

On the financing side, payables management uses supplier credit as a source of (often free) short-term financing — but stretching payables too far risks supplier relationships and forfeits cash discounts. When operations need more short-term cash than payables provide, firms draw on a line of credit, issue commercial paper (large, creditworthy firms), or factor/pledge receivables. Each source has a cost and a risk profile, and the CFO chooses the mix that funds the cash conversion cycle at the lowest sustainable cost — the practical counterpart to the capital-structure decisions from earlier units.

Working-capital financing strategies

Finally, the firm chooses how to finance current assets. A conservative strategy funds even temporary needs with long-term capital — lower risk (no refinancing pressure) but higher cost. An aggressive strategy funds some permanent current assets with short-term debt — lower cost but higher refinancing and interest-rate risk. The matching (maturity-hedging) principle finances temporary needs with short-term sources and permanent needs with long-term sources — aligning the life of the financing with the life of the asset. The choice trades cost against the risk of a cash squeeze, the recurring theme of short-term finance.

Float and the mechanics of collection

Cash management exploits float — the gap between when a payment is initiated and when the cash actually clears. Collection float delays the firm's receipt of customer payments; speeding it up (via lockboxes that receive payments directly at a bank, and electronic transfer) accelerates available cash. Disbursement float works the other way. As electronic payments shrink float, the emphasis shifts from playing the float to forecasting accuracy and concentrating cash efficiently. The principle endures: getting cash in faster and timing payments out sensibly improves liquidity without changing profitability. Concentration banking then pools cash from multiple accounts into one, so the firm can invest or deploy its full balance rather than leaving idle pockets scattered across banks.

Liquidity reserves and short-term investments

Firms hold a liquidity reserve against uncertainty, parking temporarily idle cash in marketable securities — Treasury bills, money-market instruments — that earn a return while staying highly liquid and low-risk. Sizing the reserve trades the cost of holding low-yield liquid assets against the risk of a cash shortfall. A contractor with lumpy, milestone-based cash flows needs a larger buffer than a steady-revenue business, which ties working-capital policy back to the firm's specific cash-flow pattern — the same logic the CFO lane's cash-forecasting applies.

CFO bridge

The cash conversion cycle is the single most useful concept a junior CFO can carry into a contractor's office: it explains why a company can be profitable on paper yet cash-starved, and it points straight at the levers — collect retainage, turn jobs faster, manage subs' payment terms. The CFO lane's cash-forecasting and lender-conversation workflows build directly on this chapter.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute net working capital (current assets − current liabilities) and balance illiquidity risk against idle-asset cost.
  2. Calculate the cash conversion cycle: CCC = DIO + DSO − DPO (e.g., 60 + 45 − 30 = 75 days); compute each from turnover.
  3. Manage cash (target balance, float, cash budget), receivables (credit terms, 2/10 net 30), inventory (EOQ, JIT), and payables (discounts vs stretching).
  4. Choose a financing strategy: conservative (safe, costly) vs aggressive (cheap, risky) vs matching (maturity-hedge).

Recap: working capital is the cash tied up in operations, and the cash conversion cycle (DIO + DSO − DPO, e.g. 75 days) measures how long the firm's own cash is locked up; shortening it — faster inventory turns, quicker collections, sensible payment timing — frees cash and lowers AFN; cash, receivables (2/10 net 30 credit terms), inventory (EOQ/JIT), and payables are each managed to minimize tied-up cash; and the firm finances current assets along a conservative–aggressive spectrum, with the matching principle aligning financing maturity to asset life.
